questions.q: State the primary distinguishing feature of Web 2.0 compared to Web 1.0 in one sentence.
questions.a: Web 2.0 enables user-generated content and two-way interaction (read-write), whereas Web 1.0 was primarily read-only static pages. A wrong answer (e.g., "Web 2.0 uses HTML5") reveals confusion between enabling technologies and the fundamental paradigm shift.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what "Semantic Web" means in the context of Web 3.0 and why it is not simply "better search."
questions.a: The Semantic Web adds machine-readable metadata (meaning) to data so software agents can understand relationships and automate tasks, not just match keywords. A wrong answer equating it with improved search algorithms shows the student misses the shift from document-centric to data-centric representation.

questions.q: A startup wants to build a platform where users own their identity and data, and no central server can censor content. Which web generation's principles align best, and name two specific technologies that would implement this.
questions.a: Web 3.0 principles align; technologies: blockchain (for decentralized identity/storage) and IPFS (for distributed file storage). A wrong answer suggesting "Web 2.0 with better privacy settings" reveals misunderstanding of architectural decentralization vs. policy-based privacy.

questions.q: Compare the role of the server in Web 1.0, Web 2.0, and Web 3.0 architectures. How does the trust model change across generations?
questions.a: Web 1.0: central server serves static files; trust = server authority. Web 2.0: server processes user data and runs application logic; trust = platform reputation. Web 3.0: server replaced by peer-to-peer network/smart contracts; trust = cryptographic consensus. A wrong answer that says "servers disappear in Web 3.0" misses that nodes still serve data but without central control.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "Web 3.0 is just Web 2.0 with blockchain added." Provide two technical arguments for or against.
questions.a: Against: (1) Web 3.0 introduces semantic metadata and AI reasoning layers absent in Web 2.0; (2) Web 3.0 re-architects data ownership via self-sovereign identity, not merely adding a ledger. A weak critique focusing only on cryptocurrency shows lack of grasp of the broader semantic/decentralization vision.

questions.q: Design a concept for a Web 3.0 application for Indian farmers that uses semantic data, decentralized storage, and token incentives. Sketch the three core components and one user benefit.
questions.a: Components: (1) Semantic knowledge graph linking crop, soil, weather, market data; (2) IPFS storage for immutable land records and supply-chain logs; (3) Token rewards for contributing verified data. Benefit: Farmer owns data, gets fair price via transparent market oracle. A poor answer describing a regular app with a crypto wallet shows failure to integrate semantic and decentralized aspects.
